content: The World Health Organization (WHO) publication from 2017 outlines recommendations for maternal health, emphasizing evidence-based practices to improve outcomes for mothers and newborns. The document provides detailed guidance on interventions during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period, aiming to address specific health concerns and promote positive health behaviors. 1. Copyright and Licensing: The WHO permits the use, adaptation, and redistribution of its work for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. The WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations must be licensed under equivalent Creative Commons terms. Translations must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the accuracy of the translation. 2. Guideline Development: WHO guidelines are developed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, which categorizes evidence quality as high, moderate, low, or very low. Recommendations are classified as strong or conditional based on the balance of benefits and harms, stakeholder preferences, feasibility, and equity considerations. 3. Maternal Nutrition: Pregnant women should receive counseling on healthy eating and physical activity to prevent excessive weight gain. In undernourished populations, balanced energy and protein supplementation is recommended to reduce the risk of stillbirths and small-for-gestational-age neonates. High-protein supplementation, however, is not recommended. Daily iron and folic acid supplementation is advised to prevent maternal anemia, puerperal sepsis, low birth weight, and preterm birth. Weekly supplementation may be considered in populations with low anemia prevalence if daily intake is not tolerated. Calcium supplementation is recommended to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia in populations with low dietary calcium intake. Vitamin A supplementation is only recommended in areas with severe vitamin A deficiency to prevent night blindness. Zinc supplementation is recommended only in the context of rigorous research. Multiple micronutrient supplementation, as well as vitamin B6, E, C, and D supplementation, is not recommended for improving maternal and perinatal outcomes. Pregnant women with high caffeine intake should reduce their consumption to lower the risk of pregnancy loss and low birth weight. 4. Maternal and Fetal Assessment: Full blood count testing is the preferred method for diagnosing anemia during pregnancy. In settings without this capability, hemoglobin testing with a hemoglobinometer is recommended over color scale methods. Midstream urine culture is the recommended method for diagnosing asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB). In the absence of culture facilities, Gram-staining is preferred over dipstick tests. Hyperglycemia detected during pregnancy should be classified as gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) or diabetes mellitus in pregnancy, based on WHO criteria. 5. HIV, Syphilis, and Tuberculosis: In high-prevalence settings, provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) for HIV should be routine in antenatal care. In low-prevalence settings, PITC can be considered as part of efforts to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of HIV. Systematic screening for active tuberculosis (TB) is recommended in settings with high TB prevalence. 6. Intimate Partner Violence (IPV): Clinical inquiry about IPV should be considered during antenatal visits, provided there is capacity to offer supportive responses and referrals. 7. Substance Use: Healthcare providers should ask all pregnant women about tobacco, alcohol, and other substance use during antenatal visits. 8. Fetal Growth Assessment: Routine antenatal cardiotocography and Doppler ultrasound of fetal blood vessels are not recommended for improving maternal and perinatal outcomes. One ultrasound scan before 24 weeks of gestation is recommended to estimate gestational age, detect fetal anomalies, and improve pregnancy experience. 9. A seven-day antibiotic regimen is recommended for pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria to prevent preterm birth and low birth weight. Preventive anthelmintic treatment is recommended in endemic areas after the first trimester. Eligible pregnant women should receive tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines and trivalent inactivated influenza vaccines during pregnancy. 10. Malaria Prevention: In malaria-endemic areas, pregnant women should sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets. Intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) is recommended in Africa, starting in the second trimester, with at least three doses given one month apart. 11. Common Pregnancy Symptoms: Ginger, chamomile, vitamin B6, or acupuncture can be used to relieve nausea in early pregnancy. Lifestyle and dietary advice, along with antacids, can help manage heartburn. Magnesium, calcium, or non-pharmacological options can relieve leg cramps. Regular exercise and treatments like physiotherapy, support belts, or acupuncture can prevent and manage low back and pelvic pain. Fiber supplements can relieve constipation if dietary changes are insufficient. Compression stockings, leg elevation, and water immersion can help manage varicose veins and edema. 12. Health System Interventions: Pregnant women should carry their own case notes to improve continuity and quality of care. Midwife-led continuity-of-care models are recommended in settings with well-functioning midwifery programs. Group antenatal care may be offered as an alternative to individual care, depending on preferences and available resources. Community mobilization and antenatal home visits are recommended to improve care utilization and outcomes in rural settings. 13. Prevention of Pre-eclampsia: Low-dose aspirin (75 mg) is recommended for women at high risk of pre-eclampsia, starting before 20 weeks of pregnancy. Strict bed rest and dietary salt restriction are not recommended for preventing pre-eclampsia. 14. Improving Preterm Birth Outcomes: Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended for women at risk of preterm birth between 24 and 34 weeks of gestation, provided gestational age can be accurately assessed. These recommendations are based on rigorous evidence and aim to improve maternal and perinatal health outcomes globally.
